utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. We've got until 11.45 today. We will sit and take a break for a quarter of an hour after an hour and a quarter or so. So, Mr. Milosevic, it's for you to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us continue, Mr. Bilall. Yesterday, you said that in your village there was no KLA. I wish to remind you of your statement, page 2, paragraph 4. I'm going to read slowly so that they could interpret it. "Towards the end of the year, the KLA established their headquarters near the mosque in order to defend the village from these frequent attacks caused by nothing in particular. The commander of the KLA in the village was Afet Bilalli (25 years old). There were about 30 KLA soldiers, about ten of which were from the village." So yesterday, I asked you what the name of the village commander was, and you said that you did not see anyone, you did not know anyone, and you also said that there was no KLA in the village. How do you explain this which you said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that there was a small group of the KLA, and they observed the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did they carry?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see what kind of weapons they had. They had hunting guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I asked you yesterday, and we left it at that because you did not answer me, that you went to Faik Limani's house. Who was in this house?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Faik Limani's four sons. I found them in the house. They were awake. Nexhat, Fatmir, and Sali, and Enver. And I went there with my son. And because of the -- we went there because the Serbian army and police were after us. And then we went from house to house to the house of Sadik Nebiu, where we found other civilians there in the barn. And in Faik's house, my son was wounded in the leg, from Bebush hill. And then we went to Sadik, and we found there 28 people, and we hid there. Serbian forces caught us and put us out in the yard. "Come out with your hands up." And they were beating us and mistreating us. This was the Serbian police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that later. You say that they were all civilians and that they wore civilian clothes. Why is it necessary for you to emphasise that they wore civilian clothes if they were civilians anyway?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were civilians. They were civilians. I found them there. They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that they -- that they had only hunting rifles. So they were shooting at the police with hunting rifles only. They didn't have any other type of rifles, did they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are we talking about? We seem to have changed track. You were asking about the civilians. Now, where are we going from there?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about those 30, as the witness had put it, soldiers of the KLA who were in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they use only hunting rifles to shoot at the police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You mustn't -- you mustn't confuse witnesses by jumping from one topic to another. It's liable to confuse them and it might confuse the Court too. Now, all we had so far -- all the witness has said was that they had hunting rifles. Now, Mr. Bilall, we're going back now to the KLA in the village who had hunting rifles, and the question was: Did they use those hunting rifles to shoot at the police? Now, this isn't a question aimed, as I understand it, at the 15th of January. It's just general. Generally, did they use hunting rifles to shoot at the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, they didn't fire at the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did fire at the police on the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian forces entered the village on the 15th of January, and the KLA tried to help us civilians, but they were unable to. With those weapons that they had, they were unable to help us. They had heavy weapons, the Serbian forces. They had armoured vehicles, cannon, Praga. They had return -- they had surrounded the hills round about, and they entered the village, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the number of KLA members who were killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some killed in the hills by -- the Serbian army and police fired into the hills and killed about eight, maybe nine. I didn't see them, but it was said that they were killed. They tried to help us civilians, but they were unable to, and they were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the number of casualties within the ranks of the Yugoslav army and police?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that later you escaped to Sadik Osmani's house because from there you had the possibility to flee into the woods safely; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't safe to go to the woods from Sadik's place because military and police forces were very near. They didn't -- they didn't let us go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I'm going to remind you. On page 3, in paragraph 2, you say: "We decided straight away to leave the barn and to go to Sadik Osmani's house that is on the outskirts of Gashi, the part of Racak, that photograph 4, annex A. This house is 100 metres away. It made it possible to flee safely into the neighbouring woods, and that is why we decided to go there." Now, tell me, what is correct, what you said just now or what it says here in the statement?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't -- it was further away. It wasn't in the woods, it was in the meadows. From there, you could get out into the hills. And there, Serbian forces pulled us out into the yard and beat us and stripped us to our underwear. The -- we were sitting there. There were 28 of us. Twenty-four were executed immediately. I was the fifth one behind. And they were all killed there by the Serbian army and police. They were killed by -- on your orders. And they pulled out Avdi's heart and put it on the ground, and one of them, they stuffed his white hat in his mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you something else. You said here that you had a safe escape from there into the woods. You and the others who were there did not escape before the police came. That's what you said just now. So then why did you not escape when you wanted to escape?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were beaten in the yard, and we were laid down on the ground one by one. And then, taking two or three steps back, they talked with their walkie-talkies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Bilall, we understand what you've been through, but the question was this: That it appears from your statement that the house you went to would provide or might have provided a safe escape into the woods, but you, in fact, went to the house and then went and joined a group in the barn. And the question is: Did you have an opportunity to escape into the woods? Could you have escaped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We had no chance to escape to the hills because we were surrounded, and there were 30 -- we were surrounded by about 30 police there in the yard, police and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all the persons who were in Limani's house with you, did they all go to Osmani's house, all of them?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you go in a group or did you move individually?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went together as a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And during this transfer, did anybody shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian police shot at the walls. We were inside, and they shot all around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you were moving from one house to the other, did the police notice you?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They broke down the doors, they broke down the cupboards, and they entered -- they entered Sadik's yard. We saw them very well through the windows. We saw that they were -- that they were all around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Haqif from Petrovo, what was he doing in your village at 7.00 in the morning when the attack started?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a guest at his uncle's. He was a visitor. He had come before the war started, two weeks previously, and had gone to Sadik there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was Haqif a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I saw him myself, and he wasn't a member of the KLA. Not one of us was a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that when, around 10.00, the policemen found your group in the village, there was shooting all the time. Do you know who was fighting against who? You say that there was incessant shooting. Between whom?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At us. The Serbian army and police were firing at the village and round it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that the KLA did not shoot; right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it shot or not. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, since you say that there was shooting all the time, when they entered your house, how come there was shooting in the village all the time and the police searched the 30 of you, took your documents, and beat you for an hour, as you had put it, and on the other hand, there was shooting all round?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were shouting from the -- they were shooting from the hills, because -- and in the yards, they killed civilians. And meanwhile, they were shooting from the hills. They were firing from armoured vehicles, and there were tanks around the village. But they started at 6.00, a little bit before 6.00 - I didn't have a watch - they were firing at the village, because they had us surrounded, all round the village. And then they came into the yard, killing civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question was if that shooting was going on, how is it possible for the police to search you and take your documents and beat you for an hour or so if there was shooting going on all round? Could you just explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were -- the police were not scared. They spoke through their walkie-talkies and said, "Don't fire where we are."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where was it that you were beaten and searched? Where was that all happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Sadik's yard, inside Sadik's yard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And was there some sort of protection there from the shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two houses and a barn. We were in the barn, and they were firing from the hills. But it didn't go -- the bullets didn't come inside the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And you stated that around noon, after this maltreatment that you referred to and after the threats, that the police let you leave in the direction of the village of Rance. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 12.00, they told us, "Go out to the hills one by one." Not to go to Rance but to go out onto the hills one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since they told you to go into the hills, that means that they didn't kill anyone in that yard of yours. They told you to go into the hills after they had searched you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. They searched us, they took our identity cards, and then they said, "Go to the hills one by one." And I heard them talking on their walkie-talkie themselves, and they said, "These are civilians," and the voice came, "Kill them all. They are unarmed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They searched you. They established that you were civilians, and they said over the walkie-talkie that you were civilians, and they let you go in the direction of the village of Rance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called the hill of Bebush, up the hill of Bebush. And we went up onto the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Nobody guarded you, nobody escorted you as you were leaving; you left on your own.

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police and army ordered us to go uphill from Sadik's yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you stated -- well, yes. They said that you should go, and you left, but they did not escort you; right? They did not go with you.

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, they didn't come. No, they didn't come from the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Ali Qazimi sat down and told the others to continue the journey without him because he was too exhausted. You were walking uphill, he got very tired, he sat down, and you continued the journey.

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the last. He was very tired, and he sat down and he said, "You others, go on." He was the last one. I didn't know that he was left there. And he didn't know that the others were executed up above. He was not 150 metres behind. He was last.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. You were going up towards the hill. You were moving, and you say that he did not know that the others had been killed above. Did you know that others or that somebody had been killed above?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't know what was happening up there. He -- he came up later, and I said, "Have you not seen that they've all been executed?" And I said, "Come, crawl over there. They've all been killed." There were about three behind me, and they went into the forest, and they survived too. There were five of us in all who survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that as you entered Godance, in the middle of the hill, you saw Serbian police wearing uniforms. And then you say that you saw only one policeman. How many policemen did you see in fact up there?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't one policeman, there were many policemen. There was a lot of shooting and executions going on. I couldn't tell you how many were -- were laying in wait up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't hear the interpretation well. It's coming very quietly. The volume is very low. So therefore, I didn't understand. How many policemen did you in fact see? You speak of a group of policemen and you also say that you saw one. So how many were there, in fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said at the end of his last answer, "I couldn't tell how many there were, how many were lying in wait up there." He said there wasn't one policeman, there were many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you feigned death for some five hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Five -- five hours I remained unmoved, just as if I were dead. It was only when it got dark that I got up. And then I saw five or six people dead around me, and I was so confused, I didn't know what to do. And then Shaban came and saved me, asked me, "Are you injured? Are you injured? Are you still alive?" And I said, "I'm okay." And I said, "I'm here. I'm okay." He told me that everyone had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, in that case, there's something I don't understand here. Mrs. Romano, yesterday, explained to us, said that you were without unconsciousness for five hours. This is how I understood her and this is what the transcript said. So were you without consciousness for five hours or did you pretend to be dead?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have lost consciousness, I don't know. There was so much shooting, I didn't even know where I was, what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Romano?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to the statement that I read, I stated that he feigned death for about five hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He feigned death. Yes. Maybe it was a mistranslation. Thank you. Anyway, it's what the witness says which counts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But during that time when you pretended to be dead, did you hear voices of policemen?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long did the policemen remain in that spot? Do you have any idea of that?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police stayed there until they'd finished executing everyone. I didn't see when they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But can you -- can you give us any idea of the time that they were there or not? It may not be possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. They were there in the middle of the night, but I don't know where they were exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But during the time in the ravine during the executions and you were feigning dead, can you help us as to how long the police were about in the ravine or not? If you can't say so, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was lying there when they were executing all the people. And then I lost consciousness, and I don't know what happened afterwards. There were seven or eight who were massacred. Then there were -- they pulled out -- one of them, they pulled out his heart alive and did other terrible things. And then I didn't see what happened afterwards. And they put -- they put a cap in someone's mouth, stuffed the cap in his mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said a moment ago that you pretended to be dead and now you're saying that you were without consciousness. So can you be more precise? Were you conscious or were you unconscious?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think he's answered that. He pretended to be dead, and he may have lost consciousness for a time. Mr. Bilall, are you all right? Do you feel you can go on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm all right. I'm all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I said were you all right to go on. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just said, and this is in your statement as well, that some of the bodies were mutilated, and just now you told us that the body of Ragip Bajrami was mutilated as well and that his heart had been ripped out of his chest while he was still alive, and you spoke of similar atrocities. Do you know that all of the reports pertaining to these dead mentioned that none of the bodies had been mutilated, and they never ever mentioned that somebody's heart had been ripped out of their chests while they were still alive. So why did you invent this?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that myself. He had no bullet injuries. I saw the knife and saw how they ripped his heart out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So therefore, who ripped his heart with a knife? Did you see that? Were there many people involved or just one person? How many?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was the police who did it themselves. I don't -- he didn't have any bullet wounds on his body. I know that. It was just the wound from the knife when they ripped out his heart. That was the only injury on his body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you actually see it happen or is it that you saw him lying there afterwards with his heart ripped out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went there and saw the body after it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear or did you see policemen and soldiers mutilating these bodies? Because you say that many bodies were mutilated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: His statement says some of the bodies were mutilated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Well, then let's pinpoint this, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many bodies were mutilated?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five or six were mutilated. Once they had been killed, they took a knife to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that when they took a knife to their bodies?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it myself. I went to see once the police -- Serb police and army had withdrawn, and I saw the knife injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what time was it when you came to see them mutilated with knives?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just after the fall of dark. It was about twilight. It was the time of twilight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that all of these experts, including international and Yugoslav ones, examined the bodies and did not find any knife wounds or hearts ripped out or the wounds that you described so far?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have put that to the witness, and he's given his evidence about it. You've put the point to him once already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there much blood around bodies?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was blood. Around all the bodies of people who had been killed, there was blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there much blood around the bodies?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please explain to me a sentence in your statement. Page 4, paragraph 3, line 5: "Most of the dead were in a large group, and it was obvious they were hit in the same position in which the bodies were found later." What I am interested in is what do you mean when you say, "... hit in the same position in which the bodies were found later"?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all found at the same time, they weren't found later. When five or six -- when five or six of the Serb policemen entered there, they were all in a line there, one beside the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "hit in the same position in which the bodies were found," does that mean that they were lying on the ground and that they were hit as they were lying on the ground, or, rather, executed them in that position, as you say?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They weren't lying down. They were standing up. They were executed standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you saw them being executed. You personally saw with your own eyes that they were executed?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them standing on their feet. And then there were Serb forces there, and I heard the firing, and then they fell onto the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see this with your own eyes, them being executed?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it in the same way that you saw the heart being ripped out from somebody's chest, in that same spot?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment. He can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking, was that from the same spot in which they -- in which he saw the heart being ripped out from somebody's chest while the person was still alive that he saw people being executed, in that same spot?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was near, and I saw them standing and being executed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might be wrong, but maybe according to the transcript I don't believe he said he saw the heart being ripped off. I think he saw the wound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have a note that at one stage he did say that, although he later changed that and said that -- that's a matter we'll have to look at in the transcript. We can't decide it now. Mr. Milosevic, you've had now more than your hour with this witness. Is there any other topic you want to ask him about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have many more questions, because this witness is giving evidence about some, you will have to admit, fairly incredible things. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's a matter of comment by you. We accept that he is an important witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will give you 15 more minutes because of the importance of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that from there, from that spot, you went into the woods and started a fire there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you sure, then, that there were no policemen or soldiers in the vicinity that could notice this fire of yours, even from a large distance?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sure. We were up on the mountains quite a ways away, in a ravine, a type of ravine, and we made a fire. And we had water there. There was a lot of cold water, and we stayed there until the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, how did you know that there were no more policemen or soldiers in Racak?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th, at 10.00 in the morning, a man came out and cried, "Anyone up in the mountains, you can come back now because there's no more Serb police and army in the village." And Walker arrived. It was 10.00. We went down, back into the village, and I tried to get back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that you learned that 15 members of the KLA had been killed in Racak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say 15. Eight or nine. I never said 15. I didn't see them, though. They were killed up on the mountains. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here in the large paragraph on page 5 of your statement: "Further --" and before that, you say that at that point, you left the village and went to Godance on the 17 January 1999. You say that your son had left the day before. Is that the son who had been wounded in his leg?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. My son was wounded in his leg. It was the 17th when we left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say, in the beginning of this large paragraph, you say: "Further, I was told that on the 15th of January, 1999, 15 members of the KLA were killed. They were all dressed in KLA uniforms. The only one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. The English has "ten."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm talking about the figure, not the word. What I have here is a document I got from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The figure that we have is ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is this witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Serbian version says 15. I don't know what the Albanian version says, but the Serbian one says 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We must -- we must check with the Albanian. Can the Prosecution assist at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This Serbian version has been translated from Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt the English has too.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Albanian interpreters note that the Albanian version says 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: According to the interpreters, the Albanian version too has 10. So it looks as though there's been a mistranslation somewhere. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The only one from the village who had been killed was Shaqir Latifi. And then here you go on to say: "Sadik Mujota was one of the killed, and he seemed to have a uniform on him." Where was his body found?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up in the mountains. That's what they told me, at least; up in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that he was from the village of Malopoljce?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he's from Mullopolci, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what did the trenches look like, the trenches that you dug out in Racak and the vicinity? What did they look like?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a civilian. We -- with the women and children, we dug the trenches during the night because they were shooting, and we had to escape to the mountains. I don't really know what they were like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But since you dug them out, you had to see what they looked like; how deep they were, how wide they were. How many of you participated in these works?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many people participated. I helped dig them. Fifteen centimetres. Not deeper. Fifty, 50 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say 50 centimetres deep. Were these the trenches that you dug out in December or prior to that time?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. I didn't write the date down, so I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Approximately. I'm not interested in the exact date. I'm just interested in the approximate time. When was it, approximately? Was it beginning of the winter, the end of the winter, before the New Year, after the New Year, quite awhile after the New Year?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before New Year's.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us how long before the New Year? Was it two weeks, three weeks, five weeks?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably a month and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in the building of bunkers as well or only in the digging out of trenches?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just did the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who did the bunker?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I wasn't up there, I was up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that Walker and the others from the mission were there when you came back; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the 17th of January. Or was it the 16th of January?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the 16th. You say that you came to the village around 10.00. Did you speak to him immediately after that?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't talk, but I saw him and he saw me, but we didn't talk because I wasn't feeling well. And he gestured -- he gestured to me to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was that, approximately? Around 10.00, if I understand what it says here correctly.

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 11.00 on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So he did not speak to you because you were not feeling well, but did he talk to everybody else, to all the other villagers?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did. He spoke to the other villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him speaking to the members of the KLA as well who were in the village then?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I only saw him talking to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any members of the KLA at all in the village when you came back and when Walker was there? Were there any in the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I'd come down from the mountains, I didn't see anybody but civilians and Walker, and then I went home. And then I didn't see anything more. Until the 17th, I didn't get up at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That was on the 16th. Let's not confuse the dates. I understand that this was on the 16th. Isn't that right? The following day, the day after the events that took place in Racak.

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. On the 16th, I came down from the hills on the -- at 10.00, and it was then that I went down -- went down to the village and met these people. And then I went back home, and I didn't go out of my house again. I left home the next day, on the 17th, and I left the mosque neighbourhood and went down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who took Walker and his people, his associates, to the place where the bodies were, the ravine?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all came -- they all came, and they went everywhere, and they inspected everywhere, everywhere in the village and in the ravine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they did it on their own. Nobody took them there. Or did some of the locals take them there?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone from the village took them. One of the leading people in the village took them. I didn't see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How many of you were there in that group as you were walking towards the ravine? How many of you were there? You were in the house together, you went out, you went up there, you walked uphill, you went to Rance. How many of you were there in this group?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty-four executed, five of us survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your time is now over, and we've already gone and dealt with the incident in the ravine. Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to put just a few questions to Mr. Bilall. Just a few questions, Mr. Bilall. If I have understood things correctly, when you left the yard of Sadik Osmani, the police stayed in the yard. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Court what is the distance between that yard and this ravine where the things that you spoke about happened?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how far it is from the Bebush hill to Sadik's yard. I don't know, but it's quite a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How much time did you need? Can you tell us that, how much time it took? If it was quite a distance, how much time did you need to get from one place to the other?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't all that far. It was -- but it was uphill. It took about 20 minutes, but it was slowly uphill. It was 20, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All this time there was no police and no soldiers near you as you were walking towards that place; right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police remained there in the yard, and they said, "You, go up the hill." And they remained down below.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I've understood that. So while you were walking during those 20 minutes or so, there were no police around until you encountered them up there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there were none until we went up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As you were walking, did you consider the possibility of going to different houses in smaller groups and not going all of you together in the same direction? Did you consider not doing what the police had told you to do?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we didn't dare. The police said, "Go straight up to the hills." We were all together in a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I've understood that. Thank you. But I'm interested in the following: You said that your son was wounded in the yard. Was this a serious wound? Was he bleeding?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was bleeding a little, but they tied his wounds. The people round about tied his wounds, and he was able to walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was he walking with you or what happened to this son of yours?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to Sadik's house with me, and when we went into the yard, thrown out by the police, he was in the yard with me. And there was a boy, Halim his name was, 12 years old, and he was crying. And the police put him up against the wall and asked him, "Which one of you have weapons?" And my son said, "We don't have any weapons. We are civilians, and we have come in amongst these houses to take shelter." And they took this boy Halim and my son, and they put them in another house with the women.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your son is alive, right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photograph that depicts what Mr. Halil spoke about, could I please tender that? That is photograph number 8. I would like to have it exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think they are already exhibited, and I have here a colour copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have the colour then, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in photograph number 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with that, in your written statement on page 3, paragraph 6 of the English version, you said the following: "At that moment, I looked up, up the ravine, and I noticed a policeman squatting and shooting in our direction. I think that he was the most responsible person for the killing of those who were nearest to me. Photograph number 8 depicts the position of the policeman who was shooting in our direction." Is that the place from which the policeman was shooting? He was fully in the ravine? He was not on the side, he was at this spot that you've pointed out; right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just look at the photograph beside you. You'll be able to see more clearly. Mr. Usher, would you just -- yes. Put it in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So that is where the policeman was, the one who was most responsible, the one who shot at you most, right? From that place? He was there, he was fully in the ravine, right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's here where the police shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. But the photograph, I mean the way you showed it on the spot, you stood at the place where the policeman had been. That is what you showed the investigators. Not on the side. Not on the place that you're showing now.

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were here and here. From here, from this point, they came, and from here and from there. But there was a line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, sir. Just look at the photograph. This is the photograph that you saw before. This is the photograph that was made according to your instructions. The policeman that did most of the shooting, was he in the gully at the place where you stood yourself while the picture was being taken? He wasn't on the side, right?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the photograph go back. Any re-examination, Ms. Romano?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I just have two areas, Your Honour. While the usher is still there, I would like to show another photograph. Photo number 5. And just to clarify, I think we're talking about the Exhibit 156, tab 8. And this will be photo 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Avdiu, this is the photo where you show the way or the -- the way between Sadik's house and the Bebush hill; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: This is the wrong photo. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you point -- if you can see, can you point to where was the house, the barn and the house?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here is the entrance, just here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: But in the other photo, can you see the house? Photo 5, number 5.

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Avdiu, where you are standing there in photo number 5 --

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: -- where is the house in this photo? It's downstairs -- down the hill?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Down below.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And that was the place where the policemen were?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see it here, but it's down there, down below.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And there were also policemen on the top of the hill; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the hill up there?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes. Or somewhere up on the hill.

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up there on the hill. The Serbian police was up there on the hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So they could easily shoot at you while you were going from the Bebush hill to the Sadik's house? Or the opposite, from Sadik's house to the Bebush hill?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could have done if they wished, but they knew -- they knew there was this guard up there on the hill and that they would kill them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So could you escape while you were going up the hill, you and the other persons that were in your group?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Slowly -- we went up there in a line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Avdiu, in the ravine after the shooting, you feigned death, and you remained there for five hours. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And it was getting dark, and at that time, you proceeded to check if there were other survivors? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were behind me survived, and the others were in line and were executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And that was the time when you saw some bodies, some dead people?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And you refer to mutilations. Did you see the police ripping out the heart of Bajrami or did you see the wound on his body after, when you were checking the bodies?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the police tearing out the heart, but after the police withdrew, when I had gone up there, and I saw at there was no blood from a bullet, I saw that his heart had been torn out with a knife.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you see the knife?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see the knife.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You just saw the wound; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the wound. I only saw the wound.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And Mr. Avdiu, do you have any medical training or experience?

utterances.speaker: BILALL AVDIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you ever -- did you ever -- have you ever gone to a medical school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I think you've taken this as far as you can. Yes. Thank you. Mr. Avdiu, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will take the adjournment. Is it proposed to call Mr. Abrahams next?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I had understood that the Court wanted to deal with administrative matters. I'm entirely in your hands. Mr. Abrahams would certainly like to get on in order to have a chance of getting away sooner rather than later, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are issues about his evidence which it may be useful to discuss at the outset, as to its admissibility, and I have in mind there's a great deal of history in it, which I doubt we will admit, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but we can discuss that afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position is, so far as the redacted statement is concerned, is that all those whose names had been redacted have now been contacted or are the subject of waiver by Human Rights Watch, and therefore a complete and unredacted statement is now available and I think probably has been served. It certainly can be served.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll discuss it. The sensible course may be to discuss his evidence when we return. The administrative matters may not be complete because we have only just received your disclosure document, and we require to analyse that as to the dates of the disclosure of the witnesses and as to whether we should give leave for witnesses whose evidence has not been disclosed to be called. That's one of the matters we will have to consider. We're not in a position to deal with that until we've analysed it fully. So it may be matters will be shortened. But it may be convenient to deal with administrative matters and, if there's time, to start on Mr. Abrahams if we admit him. There's an objection, of course, from the accused as to his being called at all. Yes. We'll adjourn now. Quarter of an hour, please. We'll sit again at twenty to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me deal with one matter for which we've just had notification. The accused apparently has to have further dental work next week, on Wednesday. Apparently the appointment is earlier in the morning, and we'll sit at half past nine unless he's not here, of course. We have suggested, I should point out, that perhaps the dental work could be in the afternoon. Apparently the dentist does not come in the afternoon. So there we are. That's one matter about the timetabling. What it seems sensible to do now is to discuss what we can about your application. We ought perhaps -- perhaps the most sensible way to deal with it is to look at witnesses for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have an up-to-date list on which I made some remarks myself. It already is provided. Here we are. For reasons that the Chamber is aware of, K12 has to be taken on Monday, or at least certainly started on Monday, I think. So if Mr. Abrahams were to start today and to finish today or on Monday, no problem, but there is a possibility he would have to be wrapped round K12 if there was any chance of K12 not being started on Monday, I think. But we'd hope that they'd both be finished by Monday. That then takes us to Tuesday, and the list you've got is in a slightly different format than mine. Sorry. Let's just see where we are. Then we have -- my calculations is that Mehmeti, Beqiri, and Shabani, might all be dealt with on the Tuesday. K7, who will, when here, testify without protective measures, it appears, is on Wednesday. Hendrie -- incidentally, I know the Chamber inquired about verifiers. This was a verifier, Hendrie. There is one other person who falls into a broadly similar but not an identical position, so there will be at least two serving the purpose that concerned His Honour Judge Robinson. So Hendrie on Wednesday, possibly into Thursday. Now, we don't yet know about the 92 bis status of Zhuniqi, but he could be Thursday, as could Jemini, and possibly going into Friday. Then there would be Popaj and Ramadani. Elshani we feel we may now be able to withdraw in the interest of saving time. And that will then bring us conveniently, if the estimates are accurate, to the 10th of June, which is a Monday. We will, in this process, have passed from Racak to Bela Crkva, but there will be outstanding some Racak witnesses. Walker is not available at the moment. He's elsewhere in the world, a long way away, but we are hoping that he will be able to come on the 11th or 12th of June or thereabouts. There's another man in respect of whom I raised a somewhat oblique request yesterday for a Rule 70 ruling, and I'll be able to timetable his arrival once I know the result of that request. There's then outstanding the possibility of the man Dawkins, referred to by General Maisonneuve, coming. So there are those three witnesses, who will certainly be more than two days in total, I imagine, if Walker is -- or perhaps not -- probably, if Walker is to be cross-examined at any length. That takes us to the end of next week, and then into the following week. Would Your Honour like me to press on, because we've got things timetabled right up until July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and Your Honour can see what the position is. So again, obviously the further away we get the less likely forecasts are to be accurate, but K6 on the 10th of June, then Walker maybe on the 11th and 12th, we hope, with Naumann on the 13th and 14th. That brings us then to the following week, and Vllasi, who has been disclosed, and a witness who could easily last more than one day, so we've marked him for perhaps the 17th and 18th. There's then the child witness on the 19th, although he will not take very long, I think. Hoxha, and possibly Haxhiavdij on the 19th and perhaps running into the 20th. We now being in Djakovica generally. Moving to Suva Reka on the 21st, it would be, with Berisha. And on the same 21st it seems probable or possible one could accommodate Gjogaj and also Berisha, given the strike rate we've been able to achieve. We then come to C40, also known as K35. Now, this is a witness for whom a video application is being made and will be with you almost immediately and who, I think, will be seeking a high level of protective measures, possibly closed session. In fact I think almost certainly closed session. But if he gives evidence, it will take some considerable period of time. So that the first thing that has to be organised is obviously an early resolution of those issues, because it would be a terrible waste of time for them to be resolved in a way that's adverse to his giving evidence only on the morning when there's three days set aside for him. So we must try and timetable, perhaps next week or, at the latest, the week after, any objection - and no doubt there will be objection - to the various measures sought for him. But until that happens, these are the three days set aside for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pausing there. He's got a C as well as a K number, so I guess that means he's involved in broader matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right. And I know the Chamber has the general point that I'm only seeking to call witnesses once, so some witnesses in Kosovo will cover bits of Croatia and Bosnia. And it may be inevitable that some witnesses in Bosnia and Croatia will also be capable of giving evidence about Kosovo. But if I just stay with C40, there is the possibility of one other witness seeking video facilities in the same location as C40. That isn't quite resolved yet. If he does, then -- and if we make the decision that we seek to call him, then it would be sensible to have the two witnesses dealt with together because of the resource implications for Registry and everybody else. And so it may be worth raising at least as a possibility that those three days could accommodate, or those three days running into the next day, could accommodate a further video witness, but that will have to fall for consideration a little later. We then come to C39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have got no applications, have we, in relation to these?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, not yet. These are witnesses whose availability has only recently been determined and whose attitude has only finally crystallized. But I think they will be with you today. I certainly hope so. C39 is another extended witness and we have provisionally marked three days for him, taking us into the second week of July. Can I just pause there? A general problem: With the 92 bis witnesses who were heard for cross-examination. It's been necessary, obviously, to keep a sort of supply of them here. It's a rather unattractive way of describing it, but so that we can be sure that we can fill available court time whenever time becomes available. We have no other alternative. It is a very expensive exercise. I've been given the figures by those involved, and it's having a serious effect on the budget. One possibility which I must at least mention, although I'm not sure it's appropriate in this case, would be to block out a fortnight of time, have a video in Pristina, and take them all. But assuming that's possible, and it's something that would commend itself enormously to those who have budgetary concerns as one of their major interests, assuming it's possible, it has the grave disadvantage for us that we simply then don't have a reservoir of people we can use to fill up time when witnesses go short. And with the time scale that's been imposed, it's absolutely vital that we use every available second. It may be something that can be considered, but it will come with an inevitable risk that there will be days that there will be downtime, but I mention it. So coming back to where we were. C39, into the second of July. Then we have Petritsch and Sandra Mitchell. I don't think, on reflection, that they need two days each, and so they will -- either there will be the need for 92 bis witnesses there or, alternatively, they can be bunched up a little bit. We then come to Vollebaek, who is thought to be a two-day witness. And then we come to K34, who's going to require protective measures and who, again, is allocated a substantial period of time. And so again, we must consider his application for protective measures as soon as they are properly formulated by him or those acting on his behalf so that if those days are going to be free we can know about it sooner rather than later. K33 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before we move on, is a videolink facility already installed in Pristina? Is it available?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. But I understand the technology enables it to be made available. I hope so. I mean -- perhaps I should have checked that in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't say I've actually checked the technicalities, so perhaps I should. We'll try and find that out straight away. K33 is a provisional pseudonym. I'm hopeful that that witness will be available at that time. A very important witness. We trust the provisional pseudonym may be acceptable. If he is able to give evidence then - and he's a witness who will cover more than Kosovo, much more than Kosovo - it may well be that any pseudonym will be lifted at that stage. It may also be the case that that witness will be appropriate to be taken later, but then he will, of course, be taken outside the Kosovo limited period, dealing with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, speaking for myself, if -- if witnesses are taken out of the Kosovo time and cover it, amongst other things, that would seem to me to be a perfectly proper course. The important thing is to get through the Kosovo-based -- purely Kosovo witnesses in the time allotted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Your Honour, that you're going to see, on the timetable that I've set out, that that isn't going to be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, you know the order we've made. The Appeals Chamber have supported the matter. And I think now again I must emphasise to you the importance of finishing this evidence on time and finishing this trial on time. It seems the Prosecution are not taking this matter to heart. You've heard the Trial Chamber yesterday explain that it's not simply this trial. There are other people waiting to be tried, and it's also the credibility of this institution which is at issue here. We see large numbers of witnesses still being produced. I must say for myself I question how many of them are really necessary. I think we do not need, for instance, any more political witnesses. I see the experts that you're seeking to call. I question how many of them are necessary. I notice history evidence, although the Trial Chamber has made it quite plain its view about history evidence, but I notice that Mr. Abrahams purports to cover history, although he can't really have any great knowledge about it. He's not an historian, as far as I know. And then there's sought to be called another witness. The Trial Chamber's view is this: That the Kosovo evidence should finish on the 26th of July, and it's a matter for you how you organise your evidence during that period. It may be that you'd like to reflect on this: That we had an important witness on Racak at the end, the last witness, who was actually a survivor, describe what happened. Now, it may be that that sort of evidence is more important than a large number of verifiers. Now, it's for your consideration, of course. It's your case, and how you present it is a matter for you, but the Trial Chamber wants to make it plain that there will be time limitations applied to all parties. You cannot have a trial which extends for a limitless period. Since we are on this issue, I can also tell you that we are minded to restrict the time for the accused's cross-examination for the crime-based Rule 92 witnesses to three-quarters of an hour unless there are exceptional circumstances and good cause is shown as to why it should be longer. I mention that so you should know I'm thinking about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has, of course, taken all the rulings to heart and has responded to them as best it can. It remains of the view that in this extremely large and important case, its duty is to prove its case. Its judgement on the witnesses to be called is reflected in the list that's before you. We recognise the need for public acceptance of what is happening here and respectfully draw to your attention that in the time of the case so far, the time devoted to evidence in chief, on our calculations, is 67 hours and a bit, which is, I think, something in the region of 13 full court days or 14 full court days in a conventional court and does not, in our respectful submission, amount to anything like an excessive period of time. We have a number of problems in presenting -- the other figures are these: The accused, on our calculation, until this morning's witness, 92 hours and a bit more. The amici, ten hours and a bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does that include the hours for cross-examination against 92 bis witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I have got the figures for the 92 bis witnesses on their own. 92 bis witnesses, those that relate to crime-base evidence. Those that relate to crime-base evidence, five hours and 51 minutes by the Prosecution, 26 hours and 14 minutes by the accused, 18 minutes by the amici. I'm very grateful -- just before I return to my theme, I'm grateful to the video booth who tell me the following: That videolink in Pristina is possible, but because of the limited equipment, the technical unit needs ten [sic] days' advance notice to get the material there. I'm very grateful for that. Just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I was saying, it's our duty to present this case -- and I'll deal separately with issues of experts and matters of that sort, but we have to say that not only has the Prosecution, from the first, taken every step at shortening the evidence - not all of them have been approved but they've all been taken and offered - but we very respectfully suggest that although, of course, no case can ever be perfectly presented in the leanest format, certainly the evidence we have presented has been necessary for proof of the case. I'll give you another document in a minute which I promised would come your way at some stage and it will. You cannot prove a criminal case without proving the crimes, and we have, therefore, to call the evidence. The accused doesn't admit them. They have to be proved. The document, let me just distribute that. The Court will remember at an earlier stage I indicated the sort of closing document I'd prepared. This is not something that need be, I hope, registered or anything like that, but you may find it helpful. It's intended to be. It's also heavily marked that it's draft and not for final consideration and perhaps better not to be copied or distributed, but it does that which I said I would be doing from time to time, provides an analysis under the confirmed indictment of evidence that relates to particular topics, and it's in an easily accessible format. It's called "Subject to Errors and Corrections," and you'll see from the front sheet that it's subject to witnesses that have yet to be analysed, and it may be a document that will be a useful working document to set beside other similar material being prepared elsewhere, and we're always open to correction. But you'll see if you look at, for example, pages 2 and onwards, then you have the general allegations which have been covered to some degree, significant degree. The deportation and forcible transfers start at 11, and you can see the way and the degree to which they've been covered. The transfer sites, deportation and forcible transfer sites pick up at page 53. So let's look at one of those just as an example. We have taken, at page 53, a particular paragraph, 63A, and we have set out the evidence in summary form that relates to that. And I respectfully venture to suggest that the Court will not find we have in any sense overproved any of these allegations. Killing sites at 84. For reasons we'll see when I return to the list of witnesses are, of course, at the moment, very substantially empty. 84, 85, 86, 87, 88, because we simply haven't yet had time to get through to that ms aterial. 90 is sexual assault, 94. So I hope the document will be helpful, and I hope it will satisfy the Chamber that there has been no question whatsoever of overproving this case, and indeed if there had been, we would no doubt have been alerted to that. The allegations in this confirmed indictment were themselves highly -- not selective but highly limited in the number of sites that were referred to. No suggestion of attempting to prove the whole history. Such an exercise would, of course, have been beyond our ability. So we have done our best. And I now turn to the particular problems that face a Prosecution of this sort. We have to prove the crimes. We have done it in the most economic way possible. We sought to have material taken in written or summarised form, and that's been rejected. We sought to have it 92 bis'd; that's been partially accepted, and we started off by calling one witness per site. We respectfully suggest that there is nothing more that we could have done to present this case economically and responsibly. And so the other evidence is what is important. And this brings me to another topic that I was going to raise at some stage but perhaps I can conveniently raise now. Because I fear that it is we who have the experience of preparing these cases and it is, of course, experience that won't be known to others. Cases like this, the overall case perhaps being the largest -- yes, the largest case of its kind since certainly the Second World War. Cases like this would be easy to prove shortly if there was one member of the accused's inner circle who was able to come and give fully accurate and acceptable evidence of everything that happened. Maybe the case could be proved almost by the single witness. Life isn't like that. Witnesses, the closer they get to the accused, are the more difficult to approach, the more difficult to use. When we contemplate using them, we encounter the difficulties of the particular adversarial system which is effectively premised on the basis that you have to take a witness in toto rather than saying, "Well, this bit we accept, and this bit we reject and would wish to cross-examine." That may be a course to which we will be driven in due course, but that's the sort of problem that we encounter. Indeed, the system which -- and it's no surprise to hear me saying this, the system which may not in many respects be ideally suited to this category of case, is probably to be contrasted to other systems where witnesses of that proximity to an accused, whether they like it or not, would be hauled before the examining Court and interrogated by the examining Judge or by an advocate, accepting the bits that were acceptable to the person dealing with him and cross-examined as to the balance. Well, again that may be a course, and I'll come to that in a second, that I'll press you to consider. But again, it's not something that happens, and indeed it may well be that witnesses realise -- potential witnesses realise, whether they're co-accused or co-perpetrators or just too close for comfort, that if they say only so much that is acceptable and so much that is not acceptable, they may free themselves both from the pursuit of the OTP and also from the risk of coming to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let me interrupt you for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The 12th of -- the 10th of April, I think was the date. Now, that was the order of the Court which you appealed unsuccessfully. You must work towards it. What we wish to see from the Prosecution is the -- some acknowledgement that they are working towards these orders. When I see a list of witnesses, never numbered, may I say - it would be helpful if they were in future - this list, I suppose, is about 80 or 90 long. We have called 67 witnesses, or 64 to date. When I see a list this long, I'm driven to the conclusion that no attempt is being made to comply with the order, but the Prosecution is going on in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I -- and I've been equable throughout, and I hope that's been appropriate, and in being equable at all times and always courteous, no doubt shielding the Chamber from some of the stronger feelings that lie in the heart of the lawyers and investigators dealing with this case. And being equable throughout, I cannot deny myself the duty of responding firmly to things that are quite incorrect. The suggestion that we have not been working towards these orders is wholly incorrect and I am inclined to be offended by it. We have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't be offended, Mr. Nice. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me say straight away: We have worked as hard as we can to meet a timetable that the entire Prosecution team regards as unworkable. If we can fit this case into the time that has been allowed - and if I may say so, allowed from the beginning without any particular explanation as to why 90 days or a day in July were the limits - we would have done so. We are doing our level best to meet the requirements of the Chamber, bearing in mind that it's our responsibility to prove this case, and bearing in mind that we will not be arguing that convictions are established if the material before you is inadequate. Can I return to the point you make about numbers? In our application or in our motion of the -- I'll just get the date correctly -- 2nd of May, we set out with absolute clarity in paragraph 2 the significance in terms of numbers of the development of the trial. I'll just set it out again. Originally, we sought for between 90 and 110 viva voce witnesses and 123 witnesses who would be subject to the full provisions of 92 bis, so that the total witnesses would have been 213 to 233. The Chamber allowed 90 live witnesses with the possibility of calling more on good reason being shown. We made it clear, and I'll just take you to -- again to the figures that by -- if one then counts the 92 bis witnesses, who are now heard for cross-examination, as becoming live witnesses -- sorry, I thought it was here immediately available -- I think the figure went up to about 140. Let's see if I can find it. Now -- I know where it is. At least, I think I know where it is. Yes. I'm so sorry. It's at page 6 in the relief sought. In seeking the variations of orders, 95 witnesses listed which together with the 44 already called gives a total of 139 witnesses. We have at every stage cut back on witnesses we regard as unnecessarily duplicative, and as you saw today, we continue to do so. We find ourselves, and if I can take you and your colleagues back, please, Your Honour, to the list of witnesses we were looking at where I'd got to K33 and the 17th -- 19th of July, it's instructive to note what is left. Now, incidentally, history and politics, perhaps I'd better make some observations about that straight away. History I entirely accept is covered. There's no intention to call Mr. Abrahams, for example, to deal with history. It's in his statement but there is no intention to call him, and you've now had his summary. As to an historian expert, we respectfully suggest one is required in a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have in mind one for each side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, I'm entirely -- at the moment, as you see, we've listed possibly two, Dr. Budding and Robert Donia, simply because neither can cover the whole period and Donia covers the last part of the period. But we have in mind that to set a judgement of a case like this in a historical context, and it springs from a historical context, that the Chamber needs to have available to it some work of reference. We also have in mind that Mr. Tapuskovic made it clear right at the beginning of the case, promising a paper that was to be forthcoming, that there were historical issues that he wanted covered. But that is, in a sense, a digression. If we look at where we are on the 18th and 19th of July, if I can take your eyes down the right-hand side column. Yes. If we had to stop there and simply take, in the last week, what were our best remaining witnesses, we would be unable to prove anything in respect of murder sites listed on the right-hand side; Djakovica, passing over the page, Izbica, Meja. Terrible sites where the most terrible things happened. Vucitrn and so on. And in the light of the shape of this indictment, we respectfully doubt that it would be proper for us not to seek to prove those killing sites. If we look over the page a little further and just pass beyond those parts of the indictment to see what else is outstanding from our list and about which we strive to find economies, there are, first of all, I think we come really to the experts. The military expert, you'll see that there are two listed. The financial expert who we hope will be able to cover, either at the same time or in due course, financial issues relating to all the three indictments. We then have some particular insider witnesses you can see referred to, and then, under the heading listed in a very provisional order, various names. The demography expert it seems to us is something that the Chamber would want to have. The constitutional expert we know is something, from interjections particularly by His Honour Judge Robinson a few witnesses ago, is something you will need to have. And you know, it's very interesting for us to find how, over the last several months, witnesses have been reluctant in the extreme to come to this court and to be exposed to the experience here. Not because there is any reason to doubt their testimony but perhaps for some other reasons, and we have, with considerable difficulty, located experts to help you. And they are there to help you. They're both to prove the case and to help the Chamber, to put the Chamber in a position where it can make a proper and sufficiently deep judgement.
