The MUP expert, whose report will be with us very shortly, is plainly something that will be desirable. Whether he can cross the boundaries of all three cases or three indictments, I'm not sure. Can I then say something, because Your Honours will be getting a feel for the amount of material that the Prosecution say is residual. I explained at a much earlier stage that what we would do in taking every insider witness at the earliest moment and not trying to prove things in an orderly fashion but just trying to get as much in as we could, what I explained was that there would be a residue at the end of the allotted time, and at that stage I would have to make a decision as to whether there was enough, whether I needed to apply for more or some of what was left, which is why I'm showing you what will be left. Can I take you straight away, please, to the very end of the list to tell you something that is very comforting in terms of timetable but also concerning. There are a number of listed witnesses simply listed as R. They are Rule 70 witnesses. They are undoubtedly witnesses from whom you would be interested to hear, but I must tell you at the moment that there are problems with their coming before you, and I'll explain insofar as I can in public session what they are. Rule 70 witnesses require two so-called agreements. First the agreement to provide the information for lead purposes. Second, the agreement forged between the OTP and the providing body or government that enables the witness to come. In reality, they're not agreements at all because the provider simply can say -- or can set its terms. At present, the Rule 70 witnesses forecast there are witnesses in respect of whom I do not feel able to make the requests for protective measures required of me by the provider, and so you will not be hearing from those witnesses, at present, from me. I have to say not only are they witnesses likely to be of considerable interest to the Chamber, but if they become available in any way, now or in due course, they would be likely to take, at the very least, a week but in reality a fortnight, and they -- but there it is. I'm not prepared at the moment to put my name or the name of this Prosecution to the application for protective measures required of us. Therefore, at the moment, they drop from the picture. But there is at least another potential fortnight of evidence there. So Your Honour will see the predicament or the position in which we find ourselves. A word or so again, slightly disjointed, about insiders because I touched upon the problem of insiders or people close to this accused. I touched on the oddity of the system whereby witnesses of a certain kind can effectively bar themselves or may be able to effectively bar themselves from the witness box if they're not to be subject to

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It occurs to us, trying to put ourselves, as we always do, in the chair of the Court, that there must be a significant list of names that the Chamber knows it would like to hear from. We know that at the beginning of this case one of the charges placed upon the amici curiae was to advise you of what witnesses you might wish to call under your own powers. For the resolution of this case, that's all three indictments overall. It may well be that it would be appropriate now, or in due course, for the Chamber to identify the witnesses from whom it would wish to hear - I suspect your list and ours would be pretty close, one to another - and to give thought in the particular circumstances of cases of this difficulty in calling them yourself when they would then be subject, of course, to cross-examination by all parties, to full examination of the kind that is somewhat difficult to achieve, because only in this way may we be sure that you will have the evidence. We know the evidence. We see these people. Only then will you have the evidence that is likely to give you the best and arguably the quickest route to findings, proper findings about this case. Meanwhile, we're doing what we can with insiders who have been close to this accused. It's interesting. It's a case where everybody else knows how better to deal with it than those of us who are dealing with it, and tell us how we shouldn't call this or should call that. The first witness to come, whatever people may have said about him, was one of the very few who actually had the courage to come to this court and give evidence. And slowly, witnesses are becoming braver, and the prospects are not entirely gloomy for having more and better witnesses to reveal the full truth of what happened. But it's not something that happens overnight, and we were never in a position in any part of this case to forecast calling a single witness who could prove everything against this accused. So, Your Honour, there we are. Our present position is this: On the forecast we have at the moment, and bearing in mind that we have to prove the crimes and that we have interposed, wherever possible, witnesses of a different kind who may have a more immediate value, we see ourselves by about the middle of July - and subject to some of those three-day witnesses being cancelled or not allowed, things of that sort - we see ourselves in the middle of July being several killing sites short of any evidence, short of the ability to call our experts within the time allowed although they may possibly be capable of being called in other sections, not having the time, even should we have the inclination, to seek to call the Rule 70 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many killings sites would you be short of?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll just add those up. I think it's about six. I'll just get one of my colleagues to confirm it, but I think it's about six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of a total of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Six out of 13, I think. It's about half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If everything were equal and you had all the time that you required, how long would you estimate this part of the case to take? When do you think you might finish, if everything were equal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Our calculation, and it's always an estimation because it depends on circumstances outside our control, but I think our estimation is that if we were to prove all the killing sites and assuming that the experts are admitted in the usual short form way, 94 bis, the statement goes in and they're simply exposed to cross-examination which is what, of course, we would wish for all probably bar the financial expert, is that we would require another two months, probably, to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: September, the end of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But within that time, several of the witnesses would have covered areas of Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We would then embark -- there would then have to be at least some time for consideration of, I gather, very substantial material which is being produced on Croatia and Bosnia. Now, how long, at the moment, would you think you will take over Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I recognise you probably haven't got any detailed calculations, but just give us some idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I before -- not give you a detailed calculation, explain the position and then give you what help I can. Of course, over the last several weeks the Bosnia and Croatia teams have been working flat out, producing the material and indeed producing the pre-trial brief which is served this afternoon. There has also been important and very detailed consideration given to reducing the number of locations which we will seek to prove in Bosnia and making sure that there is consistency of approach between this and the Plavsic/Krajisnik team, and that has led to a substantial reduction. I don't know how many sites it is now. It is in the order of ten municipalities only - I can't remember the exact number now - that we are going to attempt to prove - but I'll have it in a moment from someone or other. Fourteen Ms. Graham tells me, but it's reduced. The witness list, for example, has been halved. That is still, of course, one of the necessarily generous witness lists. So that very, very substantial savings have been made from Bosnia, which is probably the biggest of all the cases yet to be tried. Frankly, the answer to the timetable question, I suspect, will lie in the hands of the accused. Will he take the same attitude towards the perpetration of evidence -- evidence on the perpetration of crimes as he has taken in Kosovo or not? In Bosnia and Croatia, there is of course -- in Bosnia in particular, there is the potential for incorporating evidence from other trials where there has been cross-examination, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Assuming that he does take the same approach. I'm very interested in your admittedly guesstimate as to the length of the Prosecution's case in Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I fear I would prefer to defer that until Monday, because it is -- I know that you've been troubled, and I use the word neutrally, but -- sympathetically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm interested, Mr. Nice, because my own private view is that a trial that lasts beyond a certain length of time cannot be fair. It is very difficult for a trial that is going to last three years to be fair to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not, of course, against the principle of Your Honour's observations although I can say nothing about the particular figures that Your Honour uses, and although it's not helpful at this stage, we all know of other cases in other jurisdictions which last a very long time. But I would prefer, if I may, to reflect with my colleagues this afternoon, if there's time between now and the final touchings to the pre-trial brief to do so, and bring you an estimate on Monday of how many witnesses may be required to prove the non-crime-base part of both those other trials. Now, whatever estimate I'm then able to give is an estimate that can be varied either up, of course, if one gets additional but irrefusably valuable evidence, or down if one gets evidence of such value that it enables us to limit and reduce evidence we would otherwise have to call. But rather than provide you -- because I know you've had estimates from the Prosecutor and you've even had estimates from me in the past, rather than provide you with a figure that is not accurate, I'd rather deal with it in that way, if that's acceptable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. We cannot spend too long on these administrative matters. We need to hear evidence, and our time is practically up. But clearly it is the overall timetable which is of significance. But the importance of July the 26th is that it will enable us to -- to have time to consider - and the accused and the amici - have time to prepare for the next part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If that part of the timetable slips, it means that the whole timetable slips. We're then looking at starting Croatia and Bosnia in 2003, it may be, which cannot be satisfactory. But -- well, we need clearly to reflect on these matters, which we will do. Now, can we deal with Monday? Mr. Abrahams, is it your proposal now to call him live? We seem to have got some sort of summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me just explain the position on that in a couple of seconds. He was subject to the full provisions of 92 bis yesterday, I think, but only in respect of his redacted first statement and his unredacted second statement. Once it became clear that his unredacted statement could be served, I think those procedures have now been gone through this morning, with the helpful cooperation of the Registry. Am I right? So his unredacted statement has now been bis'd, and it would be possible for him to be taken on Monday or Tuesday as a 92 bis witness. We would like that to happen subject only to this point: That one of the important features of his evidence is that Human Rights Watch prepared several reports critical of all parties in this conflict and served them on all parties including the Yugoslav government and, I believe by his e-mail address, the accused himself. The service of those reports, of course, is important in the information it provides to the accused, his government, his embassies and so on, and is probably not covered in detail in the statements in the way that it would be helpful to present it. That evidence could be presented pretty swiftly because the exhibits are available. So we would, of course, for reasons of economy, prefer him to be taken subject to 92 bis and subject to that particular adjustment. He's available. You've now got the summary otherwise. But I will take him, of course, as quickly as I can, and I will not repeat areas of evidence which have been given by many other witnesses already. He's necessary to you, of course -- I say necessary. Certainly highly desirable to you in order that he can give the methodology of the preparation of the book Under Orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. No evidence from him about the history will be admissible. We'll look at the statement and decide how much he's -- One final point: I'm told that the witnesses for next week include four witnesses for whom leave to apply to call since they were disclosed or their statements were disclosed, summaries were disclosed after the order - Messrs. Mehmeti, Jemini, Elshani, and Avdyli - I'm told these are all witnesses outside the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These were 92 bis witnesses at the time, and it may be that their change of status was not associated with clarification in our minds of the rules that apply to them. I'll deal with it in more detail on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, our time is up. We are not making any decisions. You can address us in due course on our proposal that you should be reduced for three-quarters of an hour in relation to the crime-base witnesses unless the circumstances are exceptional. Now, unless there's anything you want to raise which must be raised today, we're going to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Nice spoke for all of one hour, in case you haven't noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I know he did, but he was dealing with matters at our request, and they are essentially Prosecution matters. You need have no concerns. Before any decisions are made which affect you or your case, you will have the chance to address us on it. But the matters that we've been dealing with are essentially matters which purely relate to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But as far as the Prosecution is concerned and the Prosecution case, we state here that there is an enormous number of some kind of secret witnesses. There is a large number that is mentioned here. I have already objected to that, and I think that this is quite untenable. Secondly, I think that at the expense of my time for cross-examination, you cannot give a privilege to the other side and they keep showering materials on us anyway. Gentlemen, do you know that I was told today that I would be getting 50 documents -- 50 boxes of documents and 50 binders? How do you imagine in any kind of proceedings and in any kind of organisation during an ongoing trial, during cross-examination, during preparations for cross-examination, that I can read 50 boxes of documents and 50 binders with this kind of organisation that you have established? Not to mention the fact that for an hour now you have been discussing some list that I haven't got at all. I simply think that, in this way, one cannot work. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has the accused got the list? I'm told you have got the list. The list of witnesses, the latest ones to be called.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I got this. This that Mr. Nice proclaimed to be some kind of crown paper, some kind of crown achievement where I see the important witnesses are the person who said for himself that he was a thief, an informant and a criminal, the one that was called K5, and Ratomir Tanic, some witness he was. So if you're trying to prove your case with witnesses like that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't comment on the evidence now. We have in mind the amount of material which is about to be served on you. We will consider what we should do about that. We will reflect on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, today, they said that they were organising a truck in order to bring in these documents. Now, in connection with Abrahams, can I just tell you a few facts so you could think about them? You did not allow an OTP investigator to testify, and this witness is not only an investigator but he also worked on conceiving and preparing the indictment itself. So his entire story is the small scale indictment, actually. Please look at his statement, page 4, and page 5. At the end of page 4. "From April -- from April, I worked as an advisor to the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY from April to June 2000 and yet again in August 2001. I carried out an investigation and made an analysis for the indictment related to Kosovo against Slobodan Milosevic and others." So this is what he mentioned, that he worked for the OTP on two occasions during those periods. He omitted to mention, for example -- look at page 1, the witness statement of Ibrahim Rugova who testified here. It says here, "Interview carried out by Fred Abrahams in the capacity of OTP investigator." This interview was conducted on the 1st and 3rd of November, and this statement was given on -- in the year 2002. So he could have included the time when he worked as an investigator for that same OTP. He should have mentioned that in his statement or, rather, he decided to keep silent about it. So you do have a man here who worked on preparing the indictment, who is the author of a book called Under Orders, and that coincides with the indictment. This was done on behalf of Human Rights Watch. He's an investigator of the OTP. He interviewed Rugova. Most of Rugova's statement is actually contained in his statement here. So I think that this entire matter pertaining to him was actually put forth by this other side over there with a propaganda purpose in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will -- we will consider that matter in due course. Now, the time has really come for us to adjourn. We will consider the admissibility of Mr. Abrahams's evidence on Monday or Tuesday, whenever we get it. We will adjourn now. Nine o'clock Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just ask that I get the order of witnesses for next week during the course of today? Could you please issue an order to that effect; that I get a list with the right order of witnesses for next week today, during the course of today rather than have this done subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it's not plain, Mr. Nice, perhaps you could get the list to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The lists have been prepared and served in the usual way, on a regular daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of June, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.50 a.m.,
